---
title: "When Not to Use Iterators"
---

# When Not to Use Iterators

Iterators are a way to write a loop, not a rule that every loop must be a chain. These are the shapes where the chain fights the problem.

## The concept

A chain is one pass, one item at a time, with the consumer at the end. It gets worse when you need several exits, two independent cursors, a look at the neighbors plus mutation, random access, or a debugger stopped on a named local.

## When the control flow has multiple exit conditions

"Stop on the third error, or on the first value over 100, whichever comes first, and remember the index" is a `loop` with `break`. Encoding it as `take_while` plus a captured counter makes the counter do control flow the reader cannot see.

```rust
fn main() {
    let rows = ["1", "200", "3", "nope"];
    let mut kept = Vec::new();
    let mut errors = 0;
    for (index, row) in rows.iter().enumerate() {
        if errors >= 1 {
            break;
        }
        match row.parse::<i32>() {
            Ok(n) if n > 100 => break,
            Ok(n) => kept.push((index, n)),
            Err(_) => errors += 1,
        }
    }
    assert_eq!(kept, [(0, 1)]);
    assert_eq!(errors, 0);
}
```

`200` is a successful parse and a reason to stop. It is not an item you filter out and then continue past. `take_while` would drop it and also refuse to tell you whether you stopped because of it or because the slice ended.

## When two cursors move independently through the same sequence

A merge of two sorted slices uses two indices. Each index advances on its own.

```rust
fn main() {
    let left = [1, 4, 9];
    let right = [2, 3, 8, 10];
    let mut i = 0;
    let mut j = 0;
    let mut merged = Vec::new();
    while i < left.len() && j < right.len() {
        if left[i] <= right[j] {
            merged.push(left[i]);
            i += 1;
        } else {
            merged.push(right[j]);
            j += 1;
        }
    }
    merged.extend_from_slice(&left[i..]);
    merged.extend_from_slice(&right[j..]);
    assert_eq!(merged, [1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10]);
}
```

`zip` advances both. That is the wrong tool. itertools `merge` hides these cursors, and it is fine when you want the result and not the lesson. When the advance rule is the bug you are fixing, keep the indices on the screen.

## When you need to mutate while inspecting neighbors

Swapping an item with the next one while you walk is a slice algorithm. An iterator that yields `&mut T` can touch one element. It does not hand you the neighbors as mutable at the same time. The borrow checker is doing the right thing.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut readings = [3, 1, 2];
    let mut i = 0;
    while i + 1 < readings.len() {
        if readings[i] > readings[i + 1] {
            readings.swap(i, i + 1);
        }
        i += 1;
    }
    assert_eq!(readings, [1, 2, 3]);
}
```

This is one pass of bubble sort, not a general sort. It is here because `iter_mut().zip(iter_mut())` does not compile: that would be two mutable borrows of the same slice.

## When the pipeline becomes unreadable

If you cannot say the chain as one sentence, break it. Assign the intermediate `Vec`, or write the loop. A chain that captures three counters, a `HashMap`, and a `break`-shaped flag is a loop that was not allowed to look like one.

A readable checkpoint:

```rust
fn main() {
    let raw = [" Ada ", "linus", "ADA"];
    let normalized: Vec<String> = raw.iter().map(|text| text.trim().to_lowercase()).collect();
    let mut unique = normalized.clone();
    unique.sort();
    unique.dedup();
    assert_eq!(normalized.len(), 3);
    assert_eq!(unique, ["ada", "linus"]);
}
```

Two steps, two names. The normalized list is still there to log when the dedup looks wrong.

## When you need random access mid-iteration

"Look at index `i + 3`" is a slice. Iterators do not go backwards unless they are double-ended, and they do not jump. `nth` skips by consuming, which throws items away.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 11, 12, 13, 14];
    let mut ahead = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..readings.len() {
        let later = readings.get(i + 2).copied().unwrap_or(readings[i]);
        ahead.push(readings[i] + later);
    }
    assert_eq!(ahead, [22, 24, 26, 26, 28]);
}
```

`get` is the bounds check. An iterator would have to be buffered by hand to see `i + 2` and still yield `i`. At that point you have rebuilt the slice.

## When you are debugging

A chain is one expression. A debugger steps by statement, and a panic inside `map` points at the closure, which is good, but the values of the previous steps are gone unless you bound them.

While you are chasing a bad row, split the pipeline:

```rust
fn main() {
    let rows = ["10", "nope", "30"];
    let mut parsed = Vec::new();
    for row in rows {
        match row.parse::<i32>() {
            Ok(n) => parsed.push(n),
            Err(err) => eprintln!("skip {row:?}: {err}"),
        }
    }
    assert_eq!(parsed, [10, 30]);
}
```

Put the chain back when the print statements are gone and the policy is "skip errors" or "fail fast" from the error-handling chapter. Leave the loop if the `eprintln` is the product, not a temporary probe.

## Summary

Use an iterator when the program is a single pass that turns one sequence into one value or one collection, and a reader can say which. Use a loop or a slice when you are steering two cursors, exiting for more than one reason, looking at neighbors, or indexing. Both are Rust. The cookbook's job is to make the chain easy to write, not mandatory.
